source.title: The Flaw of Averages: Quantifying Uniformity of Performance on Benchmarks
source.authors: Arda Uzunouglu; Tian-Jian Li; Daniel Khashabi

record.tranche_reason: The paper studies benchmark-performance uniformity (HARMONY), not held-out pretraining cross-entropy, power-law fits, extrapolation, or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. Its scale-related results concern a different measure and do not test a listed claim version.
record.gate_note: The paper reports how HARMONY varies with model size and pretraining-token budget, but HARMONY measures distributional uniformity across benchmark subdomains, not any listed claim's loss, allocation, or downstream-predictability measure. Those results are recorded under fits_no_version. References to scaling-law work are background citations, not results from those studies.
record.test_reason: The study measures HARMONY, an entropy-based uniformity of accuracy across benchmark subdomains. It reports no pretraining loss, no power-law fit, no extrapolation, no compute-optimal allocation, and no fitted downstream-versus-scale or downstream-versus-loss relationship. Its size and token-budget results concern HARMONY, a different construct, so they go under fits_no_version. Scaling-law work appears only as a citation (Ruan et al. 2024, observational scaling laws). There is no substantive discussion of the claim, so 'cites_only' fits better than the reader's 'discusses'.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors also state that larger pretraining budgets are associated with more uniform performance on average. Their headline conclusions concern benchmarks: low-HARMONY benchmarks yield aggregate scores that misrepresent broad competence and shift under rebalancing, and they recommend reporting HARMONY alongside accuracy. They state the scale trends are empirical, not causal.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates benchmark subdomain uniformity rather than reproducing a language-model loss scaling-law method.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported parameter-count/HARMONY trend varies by model family. The token-budget trend is described for OLMo 2 1B and 7B under fixed architectures.

fits_no_version.finding: Within-family association between parameter count and average HARMONY is negative for Qwen and Llama and positive for Gemma and OLMo (Fig. 5).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Parameter count alone does not predict how uniformly benchmark performance is spread across subdomains.

fits_no_version.finding: For OLMo 2 1B and 7B checkpoints, HARMONY dips early then rises with more pretraining tokens, while aggregate accuracy changes or improves only slightly (Fig. 6).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Additional pretraining tokens are associated with more uniform subdomain performance even when aggregate accuracy barely moves.

record.code_released: The authors say they will release code; no URL is stated.
record.problems: The scale-related findings concern HARMONY rather than the claim's loss or compute-allocation outcomes; the text describes these trends as empirical rather than causal. The parameter-count trends are reported qualitatively by family, and the token-budget trends are shown in a figure with no numerical values stated in the text.

untested.parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute; no loss is measured.
Extrapolation of small-run fits to larger runs.
Effect of architecture shape on loss at fixed parameter count.
Power-law form in other modalities or regimes.
Predictability of downstream performance from scale or loss. The paper does report incidental per-size accuracies for Qwen3 and Gemma 3 (App. K/L tables) but fits no scaling relationship.
Dependence of fitted exponents or allocations on setup and fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: This is a benchmark-representativeness paper with no bearing on loss scaling laws. There is a minor internal inconsistency between the Section 4.2 text and the Fig. 6 caption on the accuracy trend. Per-size accuracy tables (App. L) show accuracy generally rising with size within Qwen3 and Gemma 3, but these are not analysed as scaling results.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameter count, tokens, or compute.
Whether power laws fitted on small runs predict much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and its scaling with compute.
Architecture effects on loss at fixed parameter count.
Power-law behavior in other modalities or training regimes.
Predictability of downstream-task performance from scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of fitted scaling exponents or compute-optimal allocations on setup and fitting choices.
